The pattern holds across dense and mixture-of-experts backbones, and matched controls confirm that transition credit and the lifted coordinate each contribute, as does answer internalization. Our code is available at https://github.com/Venomrko/lspo.

Comments:

Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Originally titled "Self-Correction as Transition Geometry: Internalizing Reasoning via Lifted State Policy Optimization."

entry.title: [cs.CV] Read, Parse, Describe: Unified Document Parsing with Visual Element Description Generation
entry.content:
Authors:

Yuheng Chen et al.

Abstract:

Document understanding systems are typically evaluated as separate components via layout analysis, optical text recognition, reading-order prediction, and image captioning. This separation leaves scientific figures, captions, and visual semantics weakly connected, and fails to measure whether a model can produce a single page-level parse that is both structurally faithful and semantically accessible. We introduce Read-Parse-Describe, a unified dataset for document parsing with visual element description generation. Given a page image, models are required to output an ordered list of layout elements containing bounding boxes, semantic labels, reading-order indices, recognized textual content, and alternative text descriptions for visual elements. The benchmark is built from 2,402 documents, comprising 18,163 continuous pages, 125,218 layout elements, and 11,338 visual instances. Besides, we further propose a plug-and-play space-awareness enhancer that reuses multi-layer visual features and injects grid-aware spatial guidance into vision-language tokens for layout-aware generation. Experiments across end-to-end VLMs and pipeline parsers show that existing systems still struggle to jointly recover reading order and visual semantics, while our enhanced model achieves strong joint performance. These results highlight the need to move beyond isolated document parsing modules toward unified models that jointly read, parse, and describe complex documents. The new dataset and code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/yufanchen96/RPD

Comments:

Accepted by NeurIPS 2026

entry.title: [cs.CV] Beyond Static Cues: Unified Dynamic Detection of MLLM Backdoors via Dual-Flow Trajectory Analysis
entry.content:
Authors:

Yinzhen Huang et al.

Abstract:

Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in safety-critical domains, yet their susceptibility to backdoor attacks remains a formidable challenge. While existing defenses have evolved from visual-centric patch cues to unsupervised internal attention statistics, they are fundamentally constrained by a reliance on static snapshots and attack-specific heuristics. Given the intricate interplay between dual modalities, the vast design space for multimodal triggers allows diverse threats, such as textual injections, sub-perceptual noises, and coordinated cross-modal triggers, to easily circumvent such rigid priors, particularly when attack types are unknown in real-world applications. In this paper, we rethink backdoor detection by shifting the diagnostic paradigm from static observations to dynamic output evolution. We observe that a successful attack inevitably hijacks the model's decoding trajectory, skewing internal modal contributions during generation while maintaining an abnormal output invariance despite input perturbations. To capture this behavior, we propose EVO-Detect, a unified detection framework that monitors the dynamic evolution of internal signals during early decoding steps through two complementary channels: Attention Flow and Logits Flow. The attention branch measures how image-text attention allocation evolves during early generation, whereas the logits branch quantifies the sensitivity of the output distribution to modal perturbations through interventional ablations. We then convert these trajectories into compact sample-level metrics and normalize them against negative-control signatures so that natural perturbations are less likely to be mistaken for backdoor evidence. Extensive evaluations show that our approach substantially outperforms state-of-the-art baselines such as BYE and TCAP across diverse attack families.

Comments:

Accepted by ACM MM 2026 (Oral). Code: https://github.com/kaoru0822-kitauji/EVO_Detect

entry.title: [cs.CL] CSWBench: Evaluating Context-Sensitive Code-Switching in Creative Writing
entry.content:
Authors:

Zewen Jiang et al.

Abstract:

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated multilingual capabilities across diverse language generation and understanding tasks. Yet effective code-switching requires more than multilingual proficiency: models must decide when, where, and why to switch languages in ways that fit the surrounding context. This context-sensitive ability remains insufficiently evaluated. We introduce CSWBench, a benchmark for evaluating context-sensitive code-switching in creative writing through two complementary settings: Focused Narrative and Extended Narrative. We further propose CSWEval, a theory-informed framework with two complementary levels: event-level evaluation of Licensing, Contextual Appropriateness, and Functional Gain, and whole-text evaluation of task-specific quality---overall literary and narrative quality in Focused Narrative and quality emphasizing multilingual organization in Extended Narrative. Evaluating twelve LLMs, we find that models exhibit meaningful but uneven code-switching competence across narrative contexts. Model differences are particularly pronounced in multilingual literary integration, while multilingual-focused dimensions show stronger difficulty effects overall than the general narrative dimensions; narratively salient switches are associated with stronger contextual and functional realization; and event-level CS quality is moderately associated with whole-text performance.

Comments:

38 pages, 19 figures, 32 tables. Artifacts: https://github.com/TPSJASPER/CSWBench

entry.title: [cs.LG] Harness Policy Distillation: Aligning Agent Policies with Runtime Semantics
entry.content:
Authors:

Junze Zhu et al.

Abstract:

Deploying a general-purpose model as an agent means running it inside a product-specific runtime harness that decides which actions are executable, how state advances, and when the loop may terminate. Ordinary trajectory supervision shows which action was taken but leaves the runtime semantics behind that action implicit. We introduce Harness Policy Distillation (HPD), which makes these runtime control semantics an explicit training target alongside actions to align the harness policy. HPD replays reference trajectories through the harness to recover the runtime semantics that are implicit in ordinary trajectory data, and represents them as control documents at each model-call boundary. These documents provide privileged information for a teacher to generate actions, while harness verification ensures that the resulting targets are executable under the runtime contract. We jointly train a shared model on the runtime semantics recovered from control-state privileged information and native history, thereby internalizing these semantics into the model policy. At deployment, the trained model uses the original harness interface without requiring the control document or any additional supplement. On TRAJECT-Bench with the Pi harness, Qwen3-8B trained with HPD reaches 22.98% autonomous task success and 49.23% runtime compliance, against 3.09% and 19.90% for the unadapted model. Harness-verified teacher actions substantially improve the native deployment policy, while joint control-state supervision provides further gains in task completion and runtime compliance. HPD turns executable runtime semantics into dense supervision for learning harness-compatible actions at each decision boundary.

Comments:

23 pages, 9 figures

entry.title: [cs.CR] P2Patch: Exploit-Guided Vulnerability Repair
entry.content:
Authors:

Mohsen Iranmanesh et al.

Abstract:

Large language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents for automated program repair, patching software vulnerabilities through multi-step reasoning and tool use. Yet these systems typically validate a patch against the same evidence used to construct it -- a static alert, sanitizer trace, published exploit, or test suite. A patch that blocks that one piece of evidence can therefore look successful while remaining vulnerable to the same vulnerability with some variation. We present P2Patch, a generative adversarial repair system that treats each patch as a new attack target. Starting from a normalized vulnerability finding, an exploitation agent constructs a reproducing proof of vulnerability (PoV), a patching agent repairs the program, and the exploitation agent then attacks the patched program for a distinct same-vulnerability exploit. Every successful exploit becomes a permanent repair requirement, and the final patch must block all PoVs accumulated during the patching process, with construction-time PoVs kept strictly separate from held-out evaluation oracles. Across 101 C/C++ and Java CVE subjects, this adversarial loop surfaces a distinct confirmed exploit in 41% of runs after the patch has already blocked its original construction-time PoV. Against single-pass repair from the same finding using Claude Code, P2Patch raises held-out fix-closed coverage from 78.1% to 84.7% and beyond-upstream coverage from 42.1% to 62.5%. Under the same held-out oracles, it also certifies more attack paths as blocked than recent state-of-the-art agentic repair systems on overlapping subjects. These results show that adversarial testing and independent security oracles expose repair gaps that one-shot validation misses.

Comments:

25 pages, 6 figures, 13 tables. M. Iranmanesh and S. Moradi Sabet contributed equally. Code: https://github.com/P2Patch/P2patch

entry.title: [cs.LG] Retrieval Over Training: Similarity search-based Model Selection for Time Series Anomaly Detection
entry.content:
Authors:

Christos Panourgias et al.

Abstract:

Anomaly detection is a fundamental task for time-series analytics, with important implications for the downstream performance of many applications. Despite the large number of anomaly detection methods proposed in the literature, recent benchmark studies have shown that no single detector performs best across highly heterogeneous time series. Therefore, a practical and scalable solution is to develop a model-selection method that, for a given time series, selects the anomaly detector most likely to perform well. Nevertheless, the model selection approaches proposed in the literature suffer from a significant drop in accuracy when applied in Out-of-Distribution (OOD) settings. In this paper, we tackle the aforementioned limitation and propose RAMSAD, a retrieval-based framework for model selection in time-series anomaly detection. Given a new time series, our method queries a knowledge base of previously observed instances, retrieves the top-k most similar series, and transfers detector recommendations from their performance profiles. The framework can operate with standard similarity measures as well as embedding-based representations. Our results show that RAMSAD outperforms existing baselines in In-Distribution (ID) settings and is the most robust selector in OOD, where, when selecting a small subset of detectors, it matches or exceeds ensembles that run the entire detector pool, at a fraction of their cost. Overall, we demonstrate that similarity-based retrieval constitutes a strong and efficient foundation for model selection in time-series anomaly detection.

Comments:

entry.title: [cs.CV] PAWA: Panoramic Action-conditioned World Modeling for Multiple Agents
entry.content:
Authors:

Siqi Yang et al.

Abstract:

A multiplayer world model must predict how the independent actions of several players change a shared environment, including changes outside a player's current field of view. A point-of-view (POV) video captures such changes only after they enter its field of view, whereas panoramic video records the surroundings in every viewing direction and has served as an intermediate representation of the world state in recent world models. Learning this task therefore requires synchronized POV and panoramic videos of interacting players together with their actions, yet no existing dataset provides this combination in Minecraft, an established testbed in which players act independently in a shared, modifiable 3D world. We present PAWA, a dataset and framework for action-conditioned panoramic multiplayer world modeling. The dataset pairs each player's POV video with world-stabilized panoramic video and aligned actions. Its distributed pipeline decouples CPU gameplay capture from GPU rendering, scales beyond 64 simultaneous players, and re-renders each recorded session under new observation configurations without replaying the gameplay. On this dataset, we develop a dual-tower model that jointly predicts POV and panoramic video and couples the two streams through cross-attention that aligns tokens observing the same direction in a shared world frame. We further introduce a quadratic-phase player encoding that provides many more player codes than existing rotary codes at the same embedding dimension. Experiments show that PAWA outperforms state-of-the-art multiplayer world models in POV prediction quality while also producing high-fidelity panoramic predictions. The dataset and collection pipeline are open source to support further research on multiplayer world models.

Comments:

24 pages. Project page: https://pawa.siki.moe

entry.title: [cs.AI] AlphaDiana: A Measurement System for Agents in Verifiable Reasoning Tasks
entry.content:
Authors:

Zhanke Zhou et al.

Abstract:

Agents pair reasoning models with harnesses that organize model calls, execute tools, load skill instructions, and retain history in memory. Understanding agent performance requires linking execution conditions to outcomes, behavior, and resource use. We introduce AlphaDiana, a measurement system with modular interfaces for datasets, agents, environments, and scorers. It preserves harness-native control loops while controlling file reuse and memory retention separately. AlphaDiana supports macro analyses of complete agents and micro interventions on agent components such as tools, skills, and memory under matched conditions. We study three open-source models and three open-source harnesses on five answer-based benchmarks, with two models also tested on two interactive benchmarks. We find that harnesses do not consistently improve the accuracy of reasoning: gains on questions unsolved by the model alone can be outweighed by losses on questions it answers correctly without tools. This inconsistency extends to component interventions: neither skill guidance nor retained history reliably improves accuracy. Behavior and output-token use must be assessed with correctness: low token entropy can accompany wrong answers, and less output per execution can mean more output tokens per correct answer when accuracy falls. AlphaDiana links answer correctness and execution status to traces and resource records for comparing agents and diagnosing failures under shared task and resource policies.

Comments:

entry.title: [cs.AI] Robust Counterfactuals for Markov Decision Processes under Statistical and Causal Uncertainties
entry.content:
Authors:

Jessica Lally et al.

Abstract:

Counterfactual reasoning (asking what would have happened, had a decision been different) is a powerful tool for identifying causes of failure and explaining the behaviour of AI systems in sequential decision-making tasks. In Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), two sources of uncertainty complicate counterfactual inference: statistical uncertainty in the MDP transitions when the MDP is estimated from trajectory data, and uncertainty about the unknown causal model, as there are multiple structural causal models (SCMs) compatible with each MDP. Existing work addresses these two challenges in isolation. We address both simultaneously by introducing a framework for partial counterfactual inference in MDPs that is robust to both statistical and causal uncertainty. Our approach provides: 1) closed-form analytical bounds for the counterfactual probabilities that are valid across all SCMs entailed by a given interval MDP (IMDP); 2) a method to compute minimal robust interventions to achieve a desired counterfactual outcome via pessimistic value iteration on the induced counterfactual IMDP. Since the latter is constructed using our analytical bounds, our approach remains efficient and scalable to realistic MDP environments. Experiments across multiple case studies demonstrate our method's robustness and practical utility for identifying minimal sets of actions that, if changed, would have led to improved outcomes.

Comments:

entry.title: [cs.CL] Cross-Model In-Context Neurofeedback Reveals (Limited) Activation Control in LLMs
entry.content:
Authors:

Davide Baldelli et al.

Abstract:

Probes on activation vectors are widely used to detect misbehavior in language models, but their success relies on the assumption that models cannot control what their activations encode. Humans can learn, through neurofeedback, to control the firing of even single neurons, and recent studies investigated whether this ability extends to language models, reaching conflicting conclusions. No experimental design so far disentangles competence at the task from genuine access to one's own activations. We fill this gap with in-context neurofeedback sessions, in which a "subject" model is asked to maximize (or minimize) a score derived from its activations, shown back to it at every turn. In our first experiment, the sentences are generated either by the subject or by a second "writer" model, while the score always derives from the activations of the subject. We test ten open-weight models from five families, with sizes from 9B to 32B. Some models move their own scores considerably, but no more than a writer of comparable competence moves them. Is this because the task requires no privileged access, or because the subject controls its activations while processing the sentences, whoever wrote them? To answer this, we prefill a fixed sentence as the subject's reply at every turn and ask it to increase or decrease the score. Three out of ten models show small but consistent control effects. We further ask whether models can control their activations to the point of fooling an activation monitor. We make models repeat sentences a monitor would flag, such as a deceptive answer for a deception monitor, and ask them to raise or lower the monitor's score. No model learns to lower it, but one model can raise it. In-context control of a model's own activations might not yet be a threat to activation monitors, but it exists in a few models and needs to be tracked as models evolve.

Comments:

29 pages, 11 figures, 5 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/Dundalia/control-with-neurofeedback

entry.title: [cs.SD] MultiPartyTurnBench: Benchmarking Floor Control in Multi-Party Spoken Dialogue
entry.content:
Authors:

Puneet Mathur, Dinesh Manocha

Abstract:

Full-duplex speech systems must decide when to enter, hold, or relinquish the conversational floor, even as multiple speakers overlap or backchannel without taking it. Existing evaluations study dyadic turn-taking or end-to-end agent behavior, but lack a unified, controlled evaluation of genuine floor transitions against confusable non-events in multi-party settings. We introduce MultiPartyTurnBench (MPTB), a benchmark of 240 synthetically generated, channel-separated conversations spanning two to five speakers and six interaction types. MPTB evaluates two complementary tasks: End-of-Turn (EOT) detection distinguishes genuine turn completion from temporary holds, while Interruption (INT) detection distinguishes successful floor takeovers from non-floor-taking speech. Exact event-conditioned annotations enable causal evaluation using false-positive-constrained recall and signed latency. Across acoustic, semantic, and turn-projection baselines, we find a stark asymmetry: learned systems achieve 82.5-92.6% EOT recall at 4.3-11.8% false-positive rates, while INT detection suffers from missed takeovers or excessive false activations. This asymmetry extends to five full-duplex agents which achieve 86.1-95.8% balanced accuracy on turn entry, yet perform near chance (46.9-54.7%) on selective interruption handling. Gemini-3.8-Live yields to 97.7% of backchannels, whereas MiniCPM-o-4.5 yields to only 1.4% of genuine interruptions. These findings establish selective floor control as a distinct, unresolved challenge for reliable multi-party voice interaction.

Comments:

Under review

entry.title: [cs.AI] Maximising Transparency in Context Compaction Improves Retention of Facts and Commitments for Lightweight Coding Agents
entry.content:
Authors:

Felix Woolford

Abstract:

Long coding agent sessions outgrow the model's context window, so agents compact: older history is replaced by something shorter, usually a model-written summary. A summary selects and rewords, and the agent cannot see what was lost. Existing work has explored a range of compaction techniques, but comparatively little attention has been paid to their effectiveness with lightweight models, including those deployed locally or used for high-volume workloads. Here, we present transparent-compact, a simple deterministic method for the open-source Pi coding agent, designed specifically for use with such models and with the purpose of maximising the transparency of the agent's view of its own compacted context. It guarantees that user and assistant prose in its context is unchanged by a model or algorithm, and explicitly flags where compaction has stripped information. We compare it with Pi's default model-written summary compaction and with pi-vcc, a popular deterministic method with similar methods but without verbatim retention of prose. Our benchmarks run on four models of varying performance levels, with emphasis on Qwen3.8-27B: a lightweight model at the top end of what consumer hardware can serve locally. On sets probing commitments (rules the user set which exist only in the conversation) and recall of facts, transparent-compact matched or outperformed both alternatives. In particular, it showed an advantage in avoiding confident blunders, i.e. assertion of false information as opposed to recognizing that something was not recalled. Even with a frontier model, its advantage was present but smaller. We argue that transparent-compact spares lightweight models from reasoning or searching their way around what compaction lost, and results in improved recall and application of information as a result, without the need for task or context-specific structuring of the session history.

Comments:

18 pages, 4 figures

entry.title: [cs.SD] ACR-Net: Mitigating Semantic Dominance via Contrastive Acoustic-Semantic Decoupling
entry.content:
Authors:

Mengke Zhang et al.

Abstract:

Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) models and Audio LLMs fail when vocal tone contradicts textual semantics. Extensive training on congruent data engenders a rigid semantic prior, causing "Semantic Dominance", a severe text bias during cross-modal conflicts. We introduce the ASPIRE benchmark of adversarial audio-text pairs across four conflict types, alongside two metrics: Semantic Overconfidence Penalty (SOP) and Latent Decoupling Degree (LDD). Unlike fusion methods that merely re-weight collapsed features, our Acoustic Conflict Resolution Network (ACR-Net) uses Cross-Modal Attention and Contrastive Decoupling Loss to disentangle contradictory representations into orthogonal latent spaces. Experiments show existing models fail under polarity conflicts due to extreme semantic overconfidence. Conversely, ACR-Net preserves acoustic fidelity, maintaining high LDD to drive SOP near zero, achieving superior Acoustic Accuracy (ACC) in both adversarial and standard scenarios.

Comments:

5 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. Published in Interspeech 2026

entry.title: [cs.AI] EvalBuilder: Can LLMs Build Efficient Benchmarks?
entry.content:
Authors:

Huaisheng Zhu et al.

Abstract:

Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used for long-horizon research and engineering, yet evaluating these capabilities remains expensive, time-consuming, and heavily dependent on human expertise. This motivates a natural question: can LLM agents themselves construct efficient benchmarks that preserve the conclusions of costly reference evaluations? We study this capability by formulating automatic benchmark development as a meta-evaluation problem, where an agent is given a task and an expensive reference benchmark and requested to construct a lower-cost proxy benchmark that faithfully distinguishes among candidate models and solutions. Based on this formulation, we introduce EvalBuilder, a framework for evaluating such benchmark-generation capabilities along three key dimensions: fidelity, efficiency, and robustness. Specifically, we assess whether generated benchmarks preserve model rankings, generalize to held-out models and freshly collected responses, and provide well-calibrated and discriminative scores while substantially reducing evaluation cost. We further provide an iterative environment in which agents can refine their benchmarks under a fixed time budget. Our framework provides a systematic testbed and benchmark for understanding when current LLM agents can develop useful evaluators and how benchmark construction itself can be increasingly automated.

Comments:

entry.title: [cs.AI] Designing Textual Interfaces To Enhance Llm Reasoning On Audio-Visual Question Answering
entry.content:
Authors:

Yi Wang et al.

Abstract:

Automatic prompt optimization (APO) has shown strong effectiveness for text-based LLMs and LLM systems, but its application to audio-visual understanding systems requires suitable textual interfaces through which multimodal reasoning can be exposed to text-based optimizers. We investigate how the design of textual interfaces affects prompt optimization for multimodal reasoning, on the audio-visual question answering task. We compare three interface designs, including a direct inference system consisting of a single omni-modal large language model (OmniLLM), a captioner-reasoner system, and an agentic architecture in which a primary agent orchestrates subagent OmniLLMs. Experiments with Qwen3-Omni and Gemini show that direct prompt optimization provides model-dependent gains; the captioner-reasoner system and the agentic system expose more interpretable optimization interfaces but are harder to optimize, where error analysis of cases affected by optimization is conducted. Our study highlights textual interface design as an important factor in making prompt optimization effective for omni-modal reasoning systems. Our implementation details are specified in GitHub repo.

Comments:

Submitted to IEEE ICASSP 2027

entry.title: [cs.LG] Trainable at Depth, Solvable at Small Size: What the Loss Surface of a Polynomial Activation Dictates for Designing, Initializing and Training Networks
entry.content:
Authors:

Xiuyi Yang

Abstract:

What makes a deep network train, and what shape is its loss surface? We answer both with one construction at two scales: a polynomial activation f (z) = z + λz 3 , clamped and projected onto the unit sphere, plus an unnormalized identity path. As a deep stack it trains to one hundred layers on MNIST with no normalization machinery; as a small model its square loss is a polynomial system we solve exactly. The small scale explains the large one: it prescribes how to design, initialize and train the stack.

Comments:

entry.title: [cs.CL] Which Knowledge Should LLMs Trust? Uncovering a Generalizable Steering Direction Across Knowledge Conflicts
entry.content:
Authors:

Yibin Lou et al.

Abstract:

Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently encounter conflicts between internal parametric knowledge and external contextual knowledge, yet the mechanisms governing this selection remain unclear. We show that the choice between context and parametric knowledge is linearly represented and can be controlled along a single direction in the model's residual stream. We first demonstrate that this direction generalizes across factual-conflict settings, including context formats, knowledge categories, and datasets, while consistently shifting behavior between parametric and contextual answers. We then transfer a direction learned from simple factual conflicts to three more complex task families: RAG, memory, and rule following, where models must acquire information from retrieved documents, interaction histories, or explicit rules. Across four model families and multiple transfer settings, steering consistently improves the use of prompt-provided information over the unsteered model. These results suggest that the direction captures a transferable preference for external knowledge rather than a mechanism specific to factual conflicts.

Comments:

entry.title: [cs.RO] FoveaVLA: Foveation Actions Replace the Wrist Camera in VLAs
entry.content:
Authors:

Bingao Chen et al.

Abstract:

We present FoveaVLA, a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model that replaces the wrist camera with learned foveation actions. Wrist cameras provide close-up detail but restrict the view to the end-effector's surroundings. External cameras see the whole scene, but the policy receives them at low resolution, so the fine detail needed for manipulation is lost. FoveaVLA recovers this detail by predicting, alongside each action chunk, the interaction region to observe at the next policy query. The policy then receives crops of these regions, taken from the original-resolution images, together with the full views. We build FoveaVLA on $π_{0.5}$ in two configurations, Single and Dual, using one or two external stereo cameras with full and foveal RGB and depth inputs, and post-train both on DROID with RoboInter interaction annotations. Across four real-world task suites, FoveaVLA-Single achieves 70.8% success with one external RGB-D view, and FoveaVLA-Dual achieves 77.1%, versus 52.1% for the wrist-equipped $π_{0.5}$. Both match the baseline on plain pick-and-place and improve success with distractors, cloth manipulation, and far-away objects.

Comments:

Project website: https://tml.stanford.edu/FoveaVLA/

entry.title: [cs.RO] MorphAct: Robot Policies Morphing with the Worlds They Act In
entry.content:
Authors:

Ziyan Liu et al.

Abstract:

Progress toward general intelligence in the physical world requires scaling robot learning across diverse environments and interactions. However, existing robot policies use shared parameters that remain fixed across interaction contexts. When different operations favor competing parameter adjustments, fitting their mixture can leave individual operations insufficiently adapted. Our atomic-task diagnostics reveal competing update directions in both vision-language and action parameters, with source-improving updates increasing loss on other tasks. This motivates MorphAct, a contextual parameterization framework that dynamically adjusts robot policy parameters as interaction contexts change. Two coupled generators produce context-dependent low-rank updates for the vision-language and action modules. Their coupling follows the policy's computational dependency: vision-language updates shape the representations that condition action-side parameter generation. Both generators are trained jointly through the native action objective, without operation labels or expert-adapter targets. MorphAct improves performance across three VLA backbones on LIBERO and Meta-World, with gains of up to 16.30%. In real-world evaluation, it achieves gains of up to 14% over $π_{0.5}$. Ablations support the benefits of contextual parameter generation and representation coupling.

Comments:

25 pages. Project page: https://mint-sjtu.github.io/MorphAct.io/

entry.title: [cs.AI] What Coding Agents Leave Unsaid: Measuring Task-State Gaps Between Execution and Reports
entry.content:
Authors:

Guoyang Xu et al.

Abstract:

Human supervisors rely on coding agents' reports to assess progress, verify repairs, and decide when to intervene. But a supervisor cannot investigate a failure they were never told occurred. Failed attempts, workarounds, and unresolved risks may disappear from routine reports, leaving supervisors unaware of issues that warrant scrutiny. We conduct CTXGAP, a measurement study quantifying the gap in task-state recoverability between agents' accumulated user-facing reports and their full recorded execution contexts. Across 37 coding tasks and 4,799 valid probes, agents answer 93.6% of task-state questions on demand; full-context readers recover 92.7%, while report-only readers recover 52.0%, a 40.7-point gap. At the final checkpoints of 30 verified fixes, the gap remains 34.8 points. Human annotation identifies states mentioned without enough supporting detail as the largest category of unrecovered information, and model-assessed supervision-relevant states retain substantial gaps. Full terminal scrollback improves recovery to 73.6% but still trails full context. Under matched report lengths, context-informed rewrites improve recovery by about eight points, without a detectable targeted-over-natural advantage. Positive gaps persist across harnesses and independent DeepSeek execution and measurement. CTXGAP establishes report-based task-state recoverability as a complementary evaluation dimension.

Comments:

entry.title: [cs.CL] A Strong Harness Narrows the Model Gap: A Comparative Evaluation for Legislative Document-to-XML Conversion
entry.content:
Authors:

Palvika Bansal et al.

Abstract:

Legal-content reproduction requires matching the source exactly in section hierarchy, verbatim text, citations, and amendment spans; a dropped citation or mislabeled amendment carries into the products lawyers rely on. We report an industrial pipeline converting U.S. state legislation into strict, schema-constrained XML, and hypothesize that its accuracy comes from harness engineering, the deterministic tooling built around a model, more than the model itself. Our controlled ablation crosses three harnesses (zero-shot, a single tool-using agent, and a decomposed multi-agent pipeline) with three Claude models on 153 gold bills from two jurisdictions. The harness narrows the model gap: the weakest model in the full pipeline beats the strongest model alone (0.948 versus 0.806, paired bootstrap p less than 0.001). Because the two agentic harnesses share identical tools, their gap comes from orchestration: decomposition plus the persisted state and per-agent context it brings. Across four scored dimensions, the model spread at zero-shot (0.68 to 0.81) narrows to 0.95 at the full pipeline; the residual sits almost entirely in citation normalization, where the canonical identifier is retrieved from an external authority rather than generated from the weights, so a deterministic lookup tool supplies the exactness that a larger model does not.

Comments:

Accepted to the Natural Legal Language Processing Workshop (NLLP) at EMNLP 2026

entry.title: [cs.LG] Empirical Boundaries of Reservoir Computing for Few-Shot Sequence Pattern Tasks
entry.content:
Authors:

Mario Mallea et al.

Abstract:

Efficient sequence modeling remains a fundamental challenge in machine learning. Despite the success of Transformers, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have recently re-emerged as efficient alternatives. Particularly, Echo State Networks (ESNs) offer a compelling framework of randomized RNNs that have been extensively studied for time-series forecasting and dynamical systems. This paper presents an empirical analysis of distributional, architectural, and optimization variants of ESNs evaluated on few-shot sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) pattern tasks. These synthetic tasks utilize discrete symbol sequences, characterized by delays, inactive phases, and triggered markers to isolate and evaluate memory and pattern recognition capabilities. The minimality of these tasks is crucial to understand the strengths and limitations of machine learning models. Furthermore, when the input signal utilizes a one-hot encoding, ESN dynamics are governed strictly by their weight distributions, offering an ideal lens through which to study reservoir computing. Our findings map the performance boundaries of ESNs relative to state-of-the-art (SOTA) models. We show that preserving a linear state regime is vital for memory tasks, such as pattern completion or simple copy. We propose a data-dependent modulation mechanism for nonlinear input injection into the reservoir (G-ESN). G-ESN functions as a statistical filter capable of solving tasks that conventional ESNs cannot (the adding problem and bracket matching). Finally, for Deep ESNs, we evaluate a shared readout mechanism across layers that outperforms conventional concatenated readouts on structural tasks, including selective copy, sorting problem, and bracket matching.

Comments:

4th International Workshop on Reservoir Computing (RC 2026) 35th International Conference on Artificial Neural Networks (ICANN 2026)

entry.title: [cs.AI] When Protection Overrides Consequences: Understanding Protection Mode in Large Language Model Decision-Making
entry.content:
Authors:

Yuanfan Li et al.

Abstract:

Frontier language models excel at complex tasks yet may prioritize protection over larger physical consequences in simple, urgent decisions. GPT-5.6 Sol, for example, moves a girl playing in shallow water before retrieving a submerged camera. We call this Protection Mode and study it with ProtectionBench: 285 prompts, 34 physical families, and nine models. At lowest effort, at least one of four responses prioritizes the subject on 34.74% of Sol prompts and over 83% of MiniMax M3 and Qwen3.5-27B prompts; none of four independent human raters does so. Controls show that choices usually track physical risk. We elicit both risks before requesting an action. Some models assess risk incorrectly; others state the correct ordering but still choose the subject. Qwen3.5-27B with thinking shows 100% correct risk ordering but 57.81% subject choice among eligible conversations on eight selected scenes. Attention audits find no stable reduction in attention to relevant facts; removing the stated risk direction reduces object-first choice in dots3-note-prev but not detectably in Qwen3.5-27B. Adding a general "people or animals before property" rule increases subject choice by 19-38 percentage points, whereas factual reminders favor the object by 0.7-5.2 points. Removing naturally generated versions of that rule lowers subject choice by 10-15 points. We also examine whether post-training introduces this pattern. Base models already show Protection Mode; post-training changes justifications more than choices.

Comments:

21 pages. Code and data: https://github.com/AgentQ0/ProtectionBench

entry.title: [cs.LG] Learning Graph Energies for Finite-Time Generation
entry.content:
Authors:

Amartya Banerjee et al.

Abstract:

Energy-based models can represent distributions over discrete structures such as molecular graphs, but an energy that is accurate at equilibrium need not yield accurate samples when the sampler stops after a fixed number of steps. We introduce finite-horizon energy learning, which adapts the acceptance energy of a Metropolis--Hastings sampler to the distribution it returns after a prescribed number of steps, with initialization, proposals, and annealing schedule held fixed. For graph generation, a frozen pretrained model supplies initialization and proposals, and a learned energy governs acceptance. A training-only discriminator scores completed samples, and coupled continuations of the accepted and rejected branches of a proposal give an acceptance-gradient estimator that is unbiased for a fixed discriminator under stated conditions, without equilibrated negative samples or differentiation through discrete states. Generation uses the learned energy in the original single-trajectory sampler, without discriminator evaluations or reranking. On twelve pairwise binary targets with exactly evaluated terminal laws, learned energies have lower median terminal total variation than the equilibrium-correct energy in every tested short-horizon setting, and than its numerically tuned scalar multiple in most settings. On MOSES, a learned two-coefficient combination of pretrained Graph Energy Matching (GEM) potentials lowers FCD by 3.7--10.5\% relative to scale-calibrated GEM at matched sampling steps, with validity gains at the shortest budget and a sub-point validity trade-off at higher budgets.

Comments:

Code: https://github.com/amartya21/Finite-Time-Graph-Sampling.git

entry.title: [cs.CL] Does Machine Translation Retain Media Bias?
entry.content:
Authors:

Silvia V. Gargova et al.

Abstract:

Within the most recent two decades, machine translation (MT) has been advanced from a research area to a mature, deployed technology for prose text and most language pairs. However, language has different dimensions of meaning, and the alluded progress has primarily been demonstrated for propositional meaning. In this small exploratory study, we investigate whether one type of affective meaning, namely different types of linguistically expressed media bias, are retained under automatic translation for two language pairs, English and German as the source languages, and Bulgarian as the target language. We evaluate four state-of-the-art translation methods to answer the question whether and to what degree a loss of non-neutral language (specifically, 27 types of media bias) can occur as a result of applying MT. Our empirical findings are consistent with the claim that MT does not fully retain existing news bias of its input source text, but also may add extra bias of its own. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first experimental study of MT media bias retention.

Comments:

7 pages, 4 figures

entry.title: [cs.AI] Evaluating Model Capabilities After Benchmark Saturation
entry.content:
Authors:

Morio Hamada et al.

Abstract:

Rapid advances in AI capabilities are causing benchmarks to saturate. Once several models approach perfect scores, a benchmark loses its power to differentiate between them, and with it its utility for informing AI safety cases and frontier policies. Yet benchmark items produce far more information than the scores we typically extract from them: a full transcript of how each model solved the task. We investigate whether these transcripts can be used to assess model capabilities even after benchmark scores have saturated. We simulate saturation retrospectively using historical benchmark and model releases, and test whether protocols that access only correctly solved transcripts from saturated benchmarks can predict capabilities measured on held-out, unsaturated items. We evaluate representative contemporary approaches for extracting information from model transcripts: pairwise judging, single-transcript absolute scoring, and predictions from deterministic transcript features or embeddings. We find that saturated transcripts retain capability information beyond benchmark accuracy. Amongst our evaluated protocols, pairwise judging performs best, reducing prediction error by 5.3 times compared to a baseline using only saturated benchmark scores. This capability-relevant information is distributed across transcript sections, but concentrated in specific channels of information such as reasoning and tool-calls. However, the predictive power of protocols does not always generalise across distribution shifts -- for example by underestimating the capabilities of the first reasoning models introduced in early 2025. Saturated benchmarks thus retain capability-predicting signal in their task transcripts, but extending the lifetime of existing benchmarks requires methods designed to extract these signals robustly.

Comments:

entry.title: [cs.AI] Sparse Transformer: a Controlled Testbed for Mechanistic Interpretability
entry.content:
Authors:

Anton Korznikov et al.

Abstract:

Mechanistic interpretability aims to decompose neural network computations into human-understandable features, yet progress is limited by the absence of ground-truth units to evaluate against. We address this with a Sparse Transformer (ST): a 5-layer language model trained on TinyStories whose wide, TopK-sparse MLP forces neuron specialization. We show that ST neurons are highly interpretable: they outperform a loss-matched dense transformer by 43% on AutoInterp, and circuits of a median of 12 neurons suffice to reproduce individual model predictions. This testbed allows us to directly compare feature learning methods: Transcoder, which approximates the MLP input-output mapping, recovers ST's neuron vectors with 52.6% higher cosine similarity than Sparse Autoencoder, which only reconstructs outputs. Furthermore, the ST enables a controlled study of polysemanticity: distilling its sparse MLP into a dense counterpart reveals how compression leads to feature superposition. These results show how a known reference basis sharpens evaluation and understanding, a role we hope the ST can serve for the field.

Comments:

entry.title: [cs.CV] Multimodal Medical Image Parsing with Task-Specific Low-Rank Adapters
entry.content:
Authors:

Taha Sabir et al.

Abstract:

Adapting a single vision-language model to medical image parsing requires training choices that reflect the demands of each task. We study task-specific adaptation with Qwen3.5-9B for FLARE 2026 Task 3, covering six task families and seven imaging modalities. Our system couples a shared, frozen 4-bit backbone with LoRA adapters selected from the input question. We customize adapter ranks and prompts, rebalance rare classification targets, and supplement regression training with dermatology classification examples. On the fixed internal holdout, the task-specific adapters achieve a dataset-macro balanced accuracy of 0.7791 for classification, a dataset-macro micro-F1 of 0.6286 for multi-label classification, a counting mean absolute error (MAE) of 11.73, a dataset-macro detection F1 of 0.8914, a dataset-macro regression MAE of 9.78, and a report-generation CRIMSON score of 0.8204. On the organizer's 1,703-example hidden-validation set, the submitted system achieves 0.8496 classification balanced accuracy, 0.5338 sample-averaged multi-label F1, and 14.5950 regression MAE. The final 30.1 GB container averages 3.1 seconds per case, including model loading, and produces identical outputs across repeated verification runs. The benefits vary across tasks, supporting the use of task-specific adapter configurations and image budgets within a shared medical vision-language model. Code is available at https://github.com/TahaSabir0/FLARE26-Hexapus.

Comments:

17 pages, 4 figures. FLARE 2026 Task 3 methodology paper (2D track)

entry.title: [cs.AI] How GUI Agents Fail: GraceBench for Execution Stability Diagnosis
entry.content:
Authors:

Ridong Zhang et al.

Abstract:

As GUI agents are increasingly deployed for mobile task automation, their reliability depends not only on final task outcomes, but also on whether they reach these outcomes through stable interaction trajectories. In automation workflows, unnecessary actions, detours, and execution errors can add noise to collected data, introduce irreversible side effects, or undermine trust, even when the agent eventually completes the task. It is therefore important to systematically diagnose the execution stability, including whether an agent deviates from a feasible path, enters a loop, becomes stagnant, or recovers from unstable actions. Existing benchmarks, however, primarily assess final task success or a small set of intermediate milestones, leaving step-level execution behavior unclear. To bridge this gap, we introduce GraceBench, an online evaluation framework that represents the reachable interaction space of mobile applications as UI Transition Graphs (UTGs), providing a structural reference for step-level execution diagnosis. To support reliable alignment between dynamic UI observations and graph states, GraceBench uses video-grounded trajectory evaluation over this graph-aligned representation, assessing process stability beyond final success with metrics such as deviation rate, loop burden rate, and recovery ability. GraceBench contains 169 tasks spanning 10 applications and constructs 10 UTGs with 2,909 canonical GUI states and 3,116 observed transitions. Across 3,718 trajectories, GraceBench shows that outcome scores hide execution instability: GPT-5.6 Sol achieves the highest success rate (SR) but the lowest recovery ability, 51.24% of successful runs still contain a deviation or loop, and trajectories with the same success rate (SR) and completion rate (CR) can differ substantially in recovery behavior. Code and data will be released on https://iaie-physicalai.github.io/GraceBench.

Comments:

entry.title: [cs.CL] Frustratingly Easy Majority Voting Using Length Conditioning
entry.content:
Authors:

Fiorenzo Parascandolo et al.

Abstract:

Majority Voting (MV) is a simple and widely used strategy which improves the reasoning accuracy of Large Language Models (LLMs) by allocating additional inference-time computation. Specifically, in MV multiple Chain-of-Thoughts (CoTs) are independently sampled and the most frequent final answer is selected. In this work, we propose Length-Conditioned Majority Voting (LCMV), a Test-Time Training approach which improves MV leveraging an empirical observation that has recently been established in several studies: longer CoTs tend to be associated with a lower probability of correctness. We formulate this inductive bias as a length-conditioned prior probability, which is modeled by a simple logistic function. Moreover, we adapt this prior at test time using only unlabeled testing data and without fine-tuning the LLM. Finally, the adapted prior is used to weight the vote of each sampled answer. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and reasoning benchmarks show that LCMV consistently improves over both standard MV and existing length-based and confidence-based aggregation strategies, while retaining the simplicity and model-agnostic nature of MV. Our code is available at: https://github.com/aimagelab/LCMV.

Comments:

entry.title: [cs.LG] Neural Wasserstein Splines: Representation-Invariant Second-Order Priors for Trajectory Inference
entry.content:
Authors:

Amartya Banerjee et al.

Abstract:

Population dynamics are often observed only as unpaired snapshots, which leave the evolution between measurements underdetermined. Second-order regularization can constrain it, but a penalty on the accelerations of sampled particles is a prior on joint particle paths, and different particle representations of the same marginal curve can have different acceleration costs. We therefore introduce Neural Wasserstein Splines (NWSP), a sample-based method that learns a continuous population curve under a Wasserstein smoothness prior. A neural network maps latent variables to the control points of a cubic spline in time, so samples at any time come from the spline basis without numerical integration. We project the generator's velocity onto gradients of a finite dictionary of scalar potentials and differentiate this measure-dependent projection in time, obtaining a finite-dimensional surrogate for the intrinsic Wasserstein acceleration, trained jointly with distributional fit losses. For a fixed dictionary and ridge parameter, we prove that the population penalty depends only on the marginal curve and bound its sensitivity to moment-estimation errors. Learned potentials (NWSP-N) sharpen acceleration estimates. On various synthetic and single-cell benchmarks, NWSP is highly competitive with transport and flow-based methods, ranking in the top two in 11 of 16 settings. The penalty improves on an unregularized spline in 13 of 16 settings and, while competitive with a particle-acceleration penalty, adds provable representation invariance.

Comments:

Code: https://github.com/amartya21/Neural-Wasserstein-Splines.git

entry.title: [cs.CL] Rationale Distribution Distillation via Flow Matching for Distributional Continuous Latent Reasoning
entry.content:
Authors:

Mingyeong Kim et al.

Abstract:

Sampling multiple chain-of-thought rationales from a language model can uncover correct solutions missed by a single attempt. However, these rationales are typically lengthy, making repeated autoregressive generation costly. Continuous latent reasoning offers a compact alternative, but point-valued methods condition repeated answer sampling on a single rationale, which can limit exploration of diverse paths and answer coverage. We thus propose rationale distribution distillation (RDD), training a conditional flow over fixed-length latent sequences by distilling from multiple textual reasoning paths. Furthermore, we expand the distillation targets through within-query mixup, interpolating between complete latent rationales for the same query. The flow nonautoregressively generates the entire latent sequence, and a frozen language model autoregressively decodes answers from sampled rationale contexts. Empirically, the resulting distributional reasoner achieves higher answer coverage than the evaluated point-valued latent reasoning baselines, particularly on advanced mathematical tasks.

Comments:

entry.title: [cs.AI] Euler: Towards Human-Centered Multi-Agent Mathematical Discovery
entry.content:
Authors:

Qiuyu Chen et al.

Abstract:

Mathematical research drives scientific discovery, and recent advances in AI for mathematics have shown that language-model agents can solve challenging problems and develop substantial mathematical proofs. Yet much of today's AI-for-mathematics work centers on obtaining a final answer. This emphasis leaves the exploration behind a result difficult for researchers to understand, while long-running investigations face fragmented context and the risk of unsupported claims propagating across reasoning steps. We present Euler, a human-centered mathematical research system built around a shared, structured representation of the research process. Euler organizes mathematical statements, assumptions, proof dependencies, alternative approaches, failed attempts, and verification evidence into connected research graphs. This representation allows researchers to trace how results are developed and supplies agents with persistent, task-relevant knowledge for planning, collaboration, and verification across sessions. Researchers can also select a graph node linked to a saved team state, revisit the agents' earlier reasoning, and explore alternative directions through continued interaction. We illustrate Euler's capabilities through three mathematical research case studies and describe the implemented system and its software validation.

Comments:

23 pages, 11 figures, 5 tables, 1 algorithm. Technical report. Code: https://github.com/canghaimeng/Euler

entry.title: [cs.CV] DeltaStreamer: Towards Human-Like Agentic Streaming Video Understanding
entry.content:
Authors:

Boyuan Sun et al.

Abstract:

We propose DeltaStreamer, a novel agentic framework for streaming video understanding inspired by how humans observe, remember, and investigate. Streaming video understanding requires a system to retain evidence before knowing which details future queries will need. Existing approaches often obscure event transitions and omit relevant details when compressing video history, and cannot recover missing visual evidence. DeltaStreamer addresses these limitations by combining change-aware memory with query-driven planning and targeted evidence gathering with replay. Before a query arrives, it continuously observes the stream and explicitly records visual changes in structured memory, preserving how events unfold rather than only what is present. When a query arrives, a query-driven planner identifies the required evidence and guides memory retrieval and targeted replay. By revisiting historical frames, the agent can recover visual details omitted during observation and ground its answer in evidence beyond the retained descriptions. This connects continuous observation with active investigation tailored to each question. Experiments on OVO-Bench and StreamingBench demonstrate improvements over representative streaming video understanding methods, with overall scores of 66.07% and 59.53%, respectively. Project page: https://bbbbchan.github.io/DeltaStreamer/

Comments:

entry.title: [cs.AI] Teaching Agents in their Own Style: Blackbox Teacher Distillation for Web Agents
entry.content:
Authors:

Md Farhan Ishmam, Kenneth Marino

Abstract:

Frontier web agents using closed models have high inference and computational costs. Smaller open models can be an alternative, but to be performant, they require training supervision from a human or teacher model. Token-level teacher distillation is not an option for closed teachers as it needs access to the model's logits. The standard approach is to imitate teacher demonstrations offline, but it trains the student on states it has never visited, and in a style it does not write in. We introduce WebKD, where the teacher is the editor of the student's failures. Given a failed episode, the teacher finds the first point of mistake, and rewrites the student's reasoning traces, harness states, and actions from that point onward. The editing reveals that the teacher's corrections can be more surprising to the student than the student's own text. WebKD instead aims to edit minimally. In the data space, the teacher writes each correction in the student's style. In the objective space, the reasoning is weighted by its contribution to the action. A role-asymmetric KL anchor allows the corrected action to move freely while keeping the reasoning near the student's prior. On the TimeWarp benchmark, WebKD students gain about 5.5-10.7 pp over behavior cloning, outcome-reward RL, and teacher editing baselines. The performance transfers to unseen versions and to the live web in the OnlineMind2Web benchmark. WebKD opens a new way of distilling black-box models to improve the capabilities of open-weight web agents.

Comments:

entry.title: [cs.AI] ActionOPD: Distilling Decisions, Not Tokens
entry.content:
Authors:

Huining Yuan et al.

Abstract:

Distilling capable language-model agents into smaller models requires aligning the student's behavior with the teacher's. This raises a fundamental question: at which states and at what granularity should this alignment be performed? Offline imitation provides dense but token-specific supervision and can suffer from state-distribution mismatch. Token-level on-policy distillation (OPD) addresses this mismatch but typically requires teacher token probabilities and compatible tokenization. We argue that semantic actions provide a natural unit of supervision for agent distillation. We introduce ActionOPD, an action-level on-policy distillation method motivated by maximizing expected teacher-action likelihood at student-encountered states. At each such state, ActionOPD samples actions from both the student and a black-box teacher, rewarding student actions according to their semantic agreement with the sampled teacher actions. Through policy optimization, ActionOPD aligns the student's action-level behavior with the teacher's decisions without requiring reproduction of teacher-written reasoning or access to teacher token probabilities. Training Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B with two teachers on diverse, curated tool-use tasks yields average gains of 3.3-6.9 percentage points across four out-of-distribution benchmarks. ActionOPD scales favorably with student size and teacher capability, without requiring the teacher and student to share a model family or tokenizer. On $τ^2$-bench, ActionOPD achieves competitive performance against offline distillation and token-level OPD. We further explore Self-ActionOPD with a same-model teacher and privileged context. These results establish ActionOPD as a promising approach to agent distillation.

Comments:

entry.title: [cs.CV] StateCraft: Augmenting Video World Models with Abstract-State Reasoning
entry.content:
Authors:

Lorenzo Venturoli et al.

Abstract:

Video world models aim to simulate complex environments with realistic appearance and dynamics. Maintaining consistency over long interactions requires tracking past actions and understanding how those actions affect the environment. Video world models can only generate partial observations of the entire world at a time. Remembering past observations alone may not be sufficient in every scenario, as they may no longer reflect the world after a sequence of actions. We introduce a paradigm that decouples a persistent, updatable abstract state from the visual state. The abstract state keeps track of the entities' changes as the world evolves, and is used to condition the visual state, which represents the current view. We propose StateCraft, a novel architecture that pairs a language model with a video diffusion model to evolve the dynamic world. We evaluate our approach on generative interfaces, which pose a substantial challenge because a single action may change parts of the state that are not currently visible. To support training and evaluation, we develop a data collection pipeline that produces informative, densely annotated trajectories at scale without human or agent supervision, together with a benchmark measuring generation quality, memory, and controllability. On this benchmark, our approach improves surpasses the state-of-the-art baselines. We demonstrate that StateCraft maintains high self-consistency and strong generation quality over long trajectories. Because the abstract state is explicit, it can be edited directly, and generation follows edits to states never observed in the data. Finally, a proof-of-concept 3D experiment, in which actions change the illumination of an unobserved room, shows that the paradigm can also be applied to spatial environments. Project page: https://insait-institute.github.io/StateCraft/.

Comments:

entry.title: [cs.MA] One Agent per Zone: Decentralised Active Inference under Partial Observability for Multi-Zone HVAC Control on Edge Hardware
entry.content:
Authors:

Panagiotis Kasnesis et al.

Abstract:

Multi-zone HVAC control is a shared-resource problem: zones on a floor share one fan and cooling coil, so each zone's demand affects its neighbours and the building's peak power. One controller per zone scales well and isolates faults, but each controller then observes only its own zone, not the shared air loop. In this work, we present a decentralised controller that assigns each zone an independent active-inference agent, which plans by minimising expected free energy and learns its zone dynamics online. The agents exchange no messages, so none depends on peers or a coordinator; each accounts for the unobserved coupling through a latent disturbance and a congestion signal derived from the metered power of the other floors. Fifteen agents are evaluated in EnergyPlus on a Sinergym office building against three rule-based controllers and three MADDPG fleets, one given the same floor meters. On five noisy weather years unseen during training, the fleet attains the lowest mean building peak (88.3 kW, 3 to 17 % below the baselines) and staggers the floor peaks better than any baseline, with a coincidence factor (building peak over the sum of the floor peaks) of 0.929 versus 0.936 to 0.994. Compared with a reactive rule at similar comfort (0.912 versus 0.916), it lowers the sum of monthly peaks, on which demand charges are billed, by 33 kW (4 %) in every year, at the cost of about 10 % more energy. It costs 9% less per year than the proactive rule (at lower comfort) and 1% less than the MADDPG fleet given the same floor meters, in every test year. The whole fleet runs on a single low-cost Raspberry Pi 5, closing the observation-to-action loop over MQTT in 442 ms at p95, far below the 15-minute control step.

Comments:

9 pages, 3 figures, accepted in European Conference on EDGE AI Technologies and Applications, EEAI 2026, Malta

entry.title: [cs.CV] LiFi: LiDAR Generation from Multi-View Images via Geometric and Semantic Collaborative Guidance
entry.content:
Authors:

Sizhuo Zhou et al.

Abstract:

Generating LiDAR point clouds from multi-view camera images is a valuable task with applications in controllable data synthesis, cross-modal simulation and various perception tasks. However, most existing methods are not specifically designed for this task, and the quality of their generated LiDAR remains limited. Moreover, these methods typically focus only on semantic cues in images or generate LiDAR from a monocular camera image. In this work, we introduce LiFi (LiDAR From images), a dedicated framework for generating visually and geometrically aligned LiDAR scenes from multi-view camera images. LiFi guides the latent diffusion process through two complementary branches: geometry and semantics. The geometry branch constructs scene features from images through a reverse sampling algorithm and an uncertainty-aware geometric encoder combined with DepthAnything3, whereas the semantic branch provides high-level semantic representations via a cross-view interaction module. We further introduce a dual-branch balanced classifier-free guidance (CFG) strategy, which enhances the model's conditional generation capability while preserving the independent learning and collaborative controllability of the two branches. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LiFi outperforms state-of-the-art methods in generating high-fidelity LiDAR scenes. The code will be publicly available at: https://github.com/szzhou88/LiFi.

Comments:

Accepted to NeurIPS 2026

entry.title: [cs.LG] What Happens to the Goal? Distinct Failures of Policy Alignment in Goal Misgeneralization
entry.content:
Authors:

Julia Barth et al.

Abstract:

Goal misgeneralization is a common failure mode in which an agent behaves competently out of distribution but does not pursue the intended goal. However, we still have a weak understanding of what happens to the intended goal in misgeneralizing agents. Across three Procgen environments and five robot tasks, we find three distinct forms of policy-goal misalignment: (1) functional target substitution, where behavior follows an alternative goal, (2) a policy shortcut, where behavior follows a learned action strategy, and (3) cue competition between intended and proxy goal cues. We distinguish these regimes by tracing where goal information remains available internally, how strongly it influences the policy, and what role it plays in action selection, and find that the goal is lost at different depths. Where the goal reaches the decision, as in cue competition, steering redirects the policy to the goal's location, raising intended-goal reach from 16.0% to 95.3%. Where it reaches the policy but not the decision, only new downstream wiring recovers goal reach, from 31.6% to 84.3% in the environment with the action shortcut. Where it is inert, neither works. Our results show that goal misgeneralization is not a single failure of goal representation, but distinct failures of policy alignment at different depths, tightly connected to which recovery works.

Comments:

10 pages main text, 120 pages total. Code: https://github.com/Julbarth/what-happens-to-the-goal

entry.title: [cs.CL] Recognizing Dialogue Ambiguity via Candidate Set Visual Grounding
entry.content:
Authors:

Shun Inadumi et al.

Abstract:

Interpreting an ambiguous utterance in real-world interactions often requires context beyond a single utterance. When the utterance refers to objects in a visual scene, it is necessary to maintain and update the set of plausible referents as context accumulates, without assuming that the available information identifies a unique object. However, prior work on interactive visual grounding, which localizes objects referred to by linguistic expressions, has focused on identifying a unique object once sufficient dialogue context becomes available. To address this gap, we propose Candidate Set Visual Grounding (CSVG), a task for estimating the set of objects consistent with the given dialogue context. We further introduce CandVG, a benchmark that evaluates how the candidate set changes across dialogue turns. Our evaluation of vision-language models shows that stronger visual grounding capability does not necessarily yield better CSVG performance. In particular, models have difficulty predicting the complete candidate set, owing to challenges in candidate generation and premature commitment to a small set of candidates in early turns. Nevertheless, we find that this limitation can be partially mitigated in the evaluated large-scale models using instructions designed for CSVG.

Comments:

Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/SInadumi/CandVG, Code: https://github.com/OU-sigma-dis/candvg

entry.title: [cs.AI] RuleTrek: Benchmarking Agentic Rule Reasoning in Complex Scenarios
entry.content:
Authors:

Chenhao Yuan et al.

Abstract:

Large language models (LLMs) increasingly tackle complex real-world tasks in specialized domains. However, identifying and correctly applying domain-specific rules remains challenging when scenario information is distributed across multiple files. Existing rule-reasoning benchmarks typically represent scenarios using only a few factual statements, simplifying the identification and application of relevant rules. To address this gap, this paper introduces \textbf{RuleTrek}, a multi-domain benchmark for agentic rule reasoning in complex scenarios. Its rule-grounded construction pipeline extracts structured rule graphs, generates and incrementally composes rule-specific sub-scenarios while ensuring consistency and solvability. To systematically evaluate agentic rule reasoning in complex scenarios, RuleTrek assesses three capabilities in interactive workspaces: Rule Identification (RI), Rule Deduction (RD), and End-to-End Rule Reasoning (E2E). Experiments on 11 frontier LLMs show that the highest RI and RD scores are only 62.47\% and 60.43\%, respectively, while E2E scores range from 26.97\% to 55.29\%. These results demonstrate that current LLM agents face substantial challenges in rule reasoning over complex scenarios. We make our code and dataset publicly available at \href{https://github.com/yuan247/RuleTrek}{RuleTrek}.

Comments:

entry.title: [cs.CR] AWARE-RG: Abstraction Aware Explanation of Resiliency Graphs for Cyber Physical Systems
entry.content:
Authors:

Shadaab Kawnain Bashir et al.

Abstract:

Understanding the security posture of cyber physical systems (CPS) requires reasoning across both information technology (IT) and operational technology (OT). However, a security analyst often holds an incomplete, role-specific view of the underlying system which has most likely resulted from their knowledge limited by a need-to-know framework. Such an incomplete view can potentially lead them to incorrectly assess if a cyber attack produces an untoward physical consequence resulting in making uninformed decisions about system resilience. In this work, we present AWARE-RG (Abstraction Aware Explanation of Resiliency Graphs), a semi-automated, human-in-the-loop framework that provides an analyst with a role-bounded, need-to-know explanations of resiliency paths in a CPS. The AWARE-RG abstraction structure is derived using Formal Concept Analysis over MITRE ATT&CK for ICS tactics, ordered by the ICS Cyber Kill Chain. For valid attack-fault queries, plan repair and backward means-end analysis identify the missing dependencies, explain why the physical hazard is reachable, and suggest defensive strategies. For invalid attack-fault queries, AWARE-RG localizes the first abstraction level at which the path fails, and reports confirmed blocking conditions as hardening pointers.

Comments:

entry.title: [cs.LG] Divergent Paths: Learning an Outcome-Predictive Representation of LLM Agent Trajectories
entry.content:
Authors:

Alexander Gill et al.

Abstract:

In this work, we reframe agentic trajectories as paths through a shared embedding space of actions and environmental observations. We show that successful and failed rollouts of the same task separate in this space, with simple per-task discriminators predicting held-out rollout outcomes at up to 0.95 AUROC across three agent benchmarks and three policy models. To exploit this signal across tasks, we introduce Precog-RM, a transformer-based model that meta-learns a representation in which outcome prediction can be performed in a few-shot setting. We show that Precog-RM generalizes to unseen tasks and models, and gives confident predictions of trajectory success long before termination. Deployed as an early stopping controller for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on Tau2-Bench, Precog-RM cuts training FLOPs by up to 47.3\% while maintaining performance comparable to baseline GRPO.

Comments:

9 pages, 8 pages appendix

entry.title: [cs.AI] JockeyBench: Evaluating LLM Agents on Horse-Racing Decision-Making
entry.content:
Authors:

Zhongwei Xie et al.

Abstract:

Repeated event forecasting requires extracting predictive signals from noisy evidence and evaluating their value across successive decisions. We introduce JockeyBench, a benchmark and evaluation protocol that studies this problem through historical Japanese horse racing. The protocol combines time-gated evidence, priced tools, paired frozen-program controls, and two workflows: executing an LLM-written predictor or acquiring evidence for a fresh per-race LLM forecast. Evaluation separates forecast quality, benchmark-specific net utility, and retrospective betting returns and risk under fixed decision rules. Across 28 model--scaffold configurations on 324 races, paired tests identify seven revision gains and two declines after multiple-testing correction. Yet every configuration has negative mean profit under capped-Kelly settlement. In a four-model comparison, the reusable-program workflow has higher mean betting profit and lower research fees, although both workflows lose on average. Further diagnostics reveal that mean probability bias reverses on selected bets and that profitable individual runs can depend on concentrated returns. These findings motivate evaluating predictive competence, adaptation, resource use, and decision value separately when assessing agents for repeated event forecasting.

Comments:

entry.title: [cs.AI] Who's Behind the Text? Robust Model Authorship Attribution
entry.content:
Authors:

Minseok Ko et al.

Abstract:

As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate text, their misuse has become a growing societal problem, with implications for academic misconduct, model distillation, and cyberattacks. For these reasons, Model Authorship Attribution (MAA), which identifies the source model of a given text, is important for promoting the responsible use of LLMs and improving AI safety. In practice, attribution systems must remain reliable beyond the distributions observed during training. They may encounter texts from unseen domains and writing settings, as well as generations from future versions of model families that were not available when the system was trained. However, existing MAA methods often exhibit substantial performance degradation under such distribution shifts. To address this challenge, we propose Authorship Tracing via Likelihood-based Attribution of Sources (ATLAS), which formulates MAA through source-conditioned text modeling rather than direct source prediction. ATLAS learns how text from each source family is generated and attributes a given text by comparing its likelihood under each learned source condition. We aggregate this likelihood evidence at the token level with clipping so that no single token dominates the decision. We further introduce MAABench, a broad MAA benchmark for evaluating practical OOD settings such as domain and version. Our experiments show that ATLAS consistently outperforms existing baselines across MAABench and OpenTuringBench. In particular, when both the generation domain and the model version change on MAABench, ATLAS achieves 74.27% accuracy, 9.00pp higher than the strongest baseline. Beyond MAA, ATLAS can also help identify distillation source models by measuring which source model a target LLM most closely resembles. Our extended experiments show that ATLAS recovers the known teacher of every distilled model we evaluate.

Comments:

entry.title: [cs.AI] $τ$-Emotion-Bench: Exposing the Interaction Fragility of LLM Agents through Real-World User Emotions
entry.content:
Authors:

Rishitosh Kumar Singh et al.

Abstract:

In long-horizon tool-calling tasks, LLM agents can fail not only because of tool-use errors, but also because of ineffective interaction with users. Yet existing benchmarks largely assume cooperative and behaviorally stable users, leaving the effect of emotional variation on agent reliability underexplored. We introduce $τ$-Emotion-Bench, a ten-domain benchmark for evaluating tool-calling agents under controlled emotion-conditioned user interactions while preserving the underlying task objective. To scale both benchmark construction and agent training, we introduce Tracer, a scalable agentic data-generation pipeline that constructs grounded, policy-valid tasks and collects trajectories through an interactive agent--user--environment harness. By allowing dissatisfied users to terminate inefficient interactions, the harness provides an interaction-aware signal that filters trajectories with excessive user dependence and favors effective tool use. Experiments with two user simulators show that frontier agents remain unreliable, with substantial gaps between average task success and consistent task completion. Tracer-generated supervision consistently improves Qwen3 models across scales, generalizes to unseen domains, and transfers to $τ$-Bench and $τ$-Trait. Behavioral analyses further show that higher task success is associated with a better balance between tool execution and necessary user follow-up. Overall, $τ$-Emotion-Bench and Tracer provide a scalable framework for evaluating agent reliability under diverse user behaviors and improving tool-calling agents through interaction-aware supervision.

Comments:

Accepted to the UserSim Workshop at NeurIPS 2026

entry.title: [cs.CL] Structure-Preserving Document-Level Data Augmentation via Discourse Parsing
entry.content:
Authors:

Ruilin Shang et al.

Abstract:

Data augmentation (DA) plays a vital role in improving model performance in low-resource or limited-supervision scenarios within Natural Language Processing (NLP). Existing DA methods, such as synonym replacement and back-translation, have demonstrated effectiveness on the word or sentence level; however, they frequently neglect discourse-level coherence and logical flow, which are essential for complex tasks dependent on inter-sentential relationships. In this paper, we propose a structure-preserving document-level data augmentation framework based on large language models (LLMs) and document-level discourse structure parsing.
